summary: A 31-foot cast-iron light on a Bridgeport breakwater, built 1894-95, moved to shore in 1919, and still an active aid to navigation in January 2020.

lens.where: Classic Fresnel lens replaced by a 155 mm modern optic in 1988 (Friends); NRHP describes a plastic Fresnel-type lens in 1989

structures.note: 31 ft; moved 1919 to a new concrete foundation about 275 ft closer to shore (NRHP; Friends says about 300 ft)

access.note: Stands on land owned by PSEG, beside its power plant; public access not yet arranged (Connecticut Post, January 2020). Tower closed (Friends).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner per Friends); City of Bridgeport applied for custody in January 2020

events.note: Temporary tubular lantern on the breakwater placed in operation 31 January 1894 (Friends; Board list gives the same date)
Permanent cast-iron tower completed; funded by the 1894 appropriation (Board 1895)
Lens lantern set up in the tower about 1 March 1895; NRHP calls it sixth order
Electrically operated gong fog signal, appropriated 1897; discontinued for repair 30 March 1898 (NRHP)
160-pound fog bell struck every 8 seconds by clockwork machine (NRHP)
Flora McNeil keeps the light after her husband dies (archive; Friends)

Breakwater demolished; tower moved to a new concrete foundation (NRHP: 275 ft closer to shore; Friends: about 300 ft)
Coast Guard proposes discontinuing and removing the light; boat owners and yacht clubs protest; plan dropped
Classic Fresnel lens replaced by a 155 mm modern optic (Friends)
Fog bell and bell-striking mechanism removed (NRHP 1989 amendment)
Offered for transfer under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act; no applications received (Friends)
Withdrawn from the transfer process over security concerns about the adjacent power plant (Friends)
Coast Guard again offers the light for transfer, calling it excess to its needs (Connecticut Post; USLHS)
City of Bridgeport announces an application for custody (Connecticut Post; USLHS, January 2020)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The breakwater temporary light went into operation on 31 January 1894; the permanent lens lantern in the tower dates to about 1 March 1895. The NRHP and the USLHS record use 1894 for the establishment and 1895 for the tower.
Connecticut Post (January 2020) calls it an active aid to navigation and Friends says it still guides mariners; the record shows inactive and does not agree.

The NRHP gives a sixth-order lens lantern established in 1895 (Item 7) and, in its 1989 amendment, calls the original lantern of 1894 fourth order. The story states both; the sources do not settle it.

The NRHP gives a 160-pound fog bell in March 1899. Lighthouse Friends gives roughly 100 pounds for the 1899 bell and describes a 1898 bell (struck every thirty seconds) that was found inefficient and unreliable before it. The story states the 160 and roughly 100 pound figures.

The NRHP gives the Board's 1906 report on the shanty and a 1904 proposal for a keeper's dwelling; Lighthouse Friends dates the shanty to 1902 and the $5,000 request to 1905. The story gives both dates.

Lighthouse Friends says a modern 155 mm optic replaced the classic Fresnel lens in 1988; the NRHP 1989 amendment describes a flashing green electric light with a plastic Fresnel-type lens. Both are stated in the story.

corrections.why: Connecticut Post, January 2020: the light is still considered an active aid to navigation; Friends describes it as still flashing green for mariners.
No source supports a 1984 build date; the nomination and Friends date the tower to 1894-95.

notes_for_editor: Present status and ownership unresolved: the newest readable sources (Connecticut Post and USLHS news, January 2020) describe the City of Bridgeport's application; no later source was read. The USCG Historian's Bridgeport Breakwater page was not readable (the live site is blocked, and the Internet Archive copy returned only the wayback frame); its search snippet is not cited. Record characteristic 'Q G' conflicts with Friends' 'flashing a green beam every four seconds'; not changed. Record focal height 9.4 m vs Friends' 31 ft focal plane (9.4 m) and USLHS 29 ft above water; not changed. First-light year: the Board's 1894 list of lights (scan p. 310) is OCR'd as 'January 31, 1804' (table read by position); 1894 is taken from Friends and matches the same Board list's other entry; the page image should be checked. Lens: NRHP says sixth order and also that it replaced a fourth-order lantern of 1894; the Board's 1895 report says only 'a lens lantern'. Left open. NRHP says the breakwater ran '11,000 feet' (OCR '11*000'); Friends says 'several hundred feet'. Not used. Move distance: NRHP says 275 ft closer to shore (and the intro says the tower originally stood 350 ft east); Friends says moved back about 300 ft. Both in story. Shanty date: Friends 1902; NRHP cites the Board's 1906 report. Both in story. Name: USLHS S. Adolphus McNeil; Friends Stephen A. McNeil (same keeper by Friends' account); USLHS form kept. Flora McNeil's 1913 newspaper article is known only as Friends quotes it; the 2006 Lighthouse Digest article by D'Entremont that Friends cites was not read. A 1913 newspaper search and a McNeil search were started but did not return within this run; no newspaper text is cited. Do not confuse with the Bridgeport Harbor light (us-ct-bridgeport-harbor), a separate tower whose keepers appear in the Commissioner reports (Hardwick, McCoart, Riley); and with the Tongue Point depot in Oregon, which the Bulletin index also lists. Norwich Bulletin 6 May 1914 p. 10 gives Flora McNeil's appointment as 'February IS. - 1965' (OCR); 1965 is impossible and the year is probably 1905; the page image should be checked. The archive gives 1904 as her start; the story says only that she succeeded her husband. The 1984 'built' event in the record has no source and is proposed for removal. Story pass 2026-10-22 (resume): the story now states the disagreements on lens order, bell weight, the move distance (NRHP 275 ft closer to shore, Friends about 300 ft back), the shanty and dwelling dates, and the lens type after 1988. The NRHP tower-construction sentence was not quoted; the story says only "cast-iron tower". The "since the keeper had to row out" wharf point is from the NRHP; the story says a small-boat wharf was built, as the NRHP says.
